subject: Agriculture
title: Soil pH
description: A short lesson to help you apply Soil pH.

hook.text: Blueberries love acidic soil. Alfalfa needs alkaline. Plant the wrong crop in the wrong pH, and it starves.

buildup.text: Soil pH measures acidity on a scale from 0 to 14. Most crops prefer a range of 6.0 to 7.5.

discovery.text: pH controls nutrient availability. At low pH, aluminum becomes toxic. At high pH, iron locks up.

twist.text: Adding lime raises pH; adding sulfur lowers it. Farmers adjust pH like tuning an instrument.

climax.text: Even a small pH shift can double or halve nutrient uptake. It's the hidden dial behind crop performance.

punchline.text: The right nutrients mean nothing if the pH is wrong.

quiz.question: What pH range do most crops prefer?

details.summary: Soil pH measures acidity or alkalinity on a scale from 0 to 14, with most crops performing best between pH 6.0 and 7.5. This topic covers how pH affects nutrient availability, what causes soil acidification or alkalinization, and how farmers manage pH through liming and amendments.
details.whyItMatters: Soil pH controls the chemical availability of virtually every plant nutrient. Even nutrient-rich soil can starve crops if the pH is wrong. pH management through liming is one of the most cost-effective investments a farmer can make.
takeaways: Most crops grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil with pH between 6.0 and 7.5
pH controls nutrient availability—iron and manganese lock up in alkaline soils
Agricultural lime raises pH while sulfur and organic matter lower it

faq.question: How does soil pH affect nutrient availability for plants?
faq.answer: At pH 6.0-7.0, most nutrients are maximally available. Below pH 5.5, aluminum and manganese become toxic while phosphorus locks up. Above pH 7.5, iron, zinc, and manganese become unavailable. Even well-fertilized soil cannot feed crops if the pH makes nutrients inaccessible.

faq.question: What causes soil pH to change over time?
faq.answer: Rainfall naturally acidifies soil by leaching calcium and magnesium. Nitrogen fertilizers and decomposing organic matter produce acids. Irrigation with alkaline water raises pH. Crop removal of base cations also acidifies soil. Regular soil testing guides pH management decisions.
